A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ViTime and RealTS. All 38 pages of v3 and 75 pages of v4, including their appendices, were readable and supported text and visual comparison. Internal reporting inconsistencies do not prevent identifying changes.

before.justification: v3 reports original ViTime forecasting, fine-tuning, ablation, robustness and computational-resource results in Section 4 and the appendices.

after.justification: v4 retains original empirical results and adds probabilistic forecasting, GIFT-EVAL evaluation, LoRA fine-tuning and denoising comparisons.

M1.justification: Sections 3.5–3.6 extend forecast outputs to histogram predictive distributions, with density/CDF definitions, variance, quantiles and prediction intervals. Appendix D.4.1 also introduces LoRA adaptation variants. The RealTS generator, tokenizer/decoder/refiner architecture and EMD-plus-KLD objective remain; Gaussian blurring and doubled temporal resolution were already documented in v3.

E1.justification: v4 adds probabilistic forecasting and GIFT-EVAL evaluation, including M4 datasets. The new ViTime-TFM training experiment uses additional data such as Favorita sales, LibCity and M4 series (Table 9). The original seven forecasting benchmarks and RealTS training remain.

E2.justification: The zero-shot comparison adds Moirai, Moment, VisionTS and ViTime-TFM, while removing the fully supervised PatchTST reference from that comparison. Probabilistic comparisons introduce Lag-Llama alongside Moirai. Fine-tuning tables add iTransformer and TimeMixer, and Figure 18 compares ViTime against TimesFM combined with three denoising methods.

E3.justification: New protocols include CRPS/ReCRPS evaluation, GIFT-EVAL MASE across horizon categories, an M4-exclusion control, and full versus LoRA fine-tuning with 1% or 10% trainable parameters. Noise testing extends to standard deviation 1.0. The dedicated ViTime-1072 comparison disappears; the standard 512-step context and four original prediction lengths remain.

E4.justification: v4 adds a training-source control through ViTime-TFM, the GIFT-EVAL M4-exclusion analysis, limited-data full-versus-LoRA fine-tuning, pre-denoising controls and stronger-noise sensitivity analysis. Existing threshold, loss, resolution, lookback and model-size ablations, missingness sweeps, attention visualizations and explosive-growth examples are retained or relocated.

E5.justification: v4 adds tabulated standard deviations for ViTime fine-tuning, numerical uncertainty values for noise and missing-data comparisons, and 50%/90% predictive intervals. v3 already contained some graphical error bars and shaded bands. Neither version specifies repeated-run counts or seeds, so the revision establishes expanded uncertainty reporting rather than an explicit increase in runs.

E6.justification: Numerous existing scores change: for example, ViTime's Electricity ReMAE changes from 0.340 in v3 Table 1 to 0.308 in v4 Table 2b. New probabilistic and GIFT-EVAL results substantially expand the evidence. Table 15 reports 38.3% long-horizon and 28.9% medium-horizon MASE improvements over TimesFM, but worse short-horizon performance. Some v4 summary scores conflict with its detailed tables, limiting performance interpretation.

T1.justification: v3 Appendix D's spatiotemporal-isometry, spectral-fidelity and geometric-regularization mathematics are replaced by stripe-SNR and Gaussian-blur-SNR theorems and proofs in v4 Section 3.4 and Appendix C. v4 also introduces predictive-distribution mathematics and ReCRPS. Existing optimal-threshold propositions are moved into the main text, while their proofs and the system-error derivations are revised.

C1.justification: The abstract, contributions and conclusion explicitly broaden the work to both point and probabilistic forecasting, including claims of state-of-the-art zero-shot probabilistic performance. The vision-based ViTime/RealTS contribution and the original 9–15% forecasting and 20–30% perturbation headline comparisons are largely retained.

C2.justification: v4 replaces much of the geometric-regularization explanation with an SNR-based mechanism. It distinguishes absolute accuracy from relative noise robustness, acknowledging faster degradation for ViTime. New discussions address limited-data overfitting/forgetting, LoRA, denoising tradeoffs, hypothesized M4 overlap and challenges in generating realistic multivariate correlations. The earlier truncation and synthetic-data limitations remain.

D1.justification: v4 discloses RealTS sampling probabilities, Adam with learning rate 2×10^-4, detailed refiner components, explicit masking/loss handling, baseline checkpoint identifiers and ViTime-TFM corpus counts. It adds code/pretrained-model access information and states that evaluation logs are released. These substantially expand v3's documentation without establishing changes to previously unspecified settings.

R1.justification: The introduction and related work substantially expand coverage of visual encodings and forecasting methods, including VisualAE, Swin4TS, VisionTS and LDM4TS, alongside additional foundation models. ViTime is now positioned against prior visual forecasting through its formal metric-space treatment, quantization theory and controlled synthetic training, rather than primarily contrasting vision with numerical fitting.

P1.justification: The introduction, related work and robustness discussion are extensively rewritten. Threshold analysis, ablations, attention interpretation and limitations move from appendices into the main narrative. Metrics receive a separate section, probabilistic forecasting is integrated throughout, and the appendices are reorganized. Authorship and publication headers also change.

P2.justification: The main text changes from two columns to one, and three architecture diagrams are consolidated and redrawn as Figure 1. Comparison tables are substantially restructured, including separate original-scale/rescaled summaries and landscape appendix tables. New noise, LoRA, denoising and predictive-distribution displays accompany relocated existing ablation and interpretation figures.

improvement.justification: Broader comparisons, probabilistic evaluation, additional controls and fuller reproducibility and uncertainty reporting offer substantial benefits. However, central results become internally inconsistent: v3 Tables 1 and 7 agree on ETTh1 ReMSE 0.490, whereas v4 Table 2b reports 0.457 while its listed values in Tables 10–14 average approximately 0.514. GIFT-EVAL prose also reverses the long/medium gains. These unresolved conflicts undermine the expanded performance evidence, preventing a reliable judgment of net overall improvement.
